analysis.one_liner: Raises fuel-efficiency requirements for light trucks, large SUVs, and federal vehicles.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; both committees referred it to subcommittees, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have phased in a fuel-economy standard for light trucks reaching 27.5 miles per gallon by model year 2007, extended fuel-economy rules to vehicles weighing up to 10,000 pounds (capturing many large SUVs), and required federal agencies to buy progressively more efficient vehicles. Light trucks had long been held to a lower standard than cars. The bill was referred to two House committees, each sent it to a subcommittee, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary drivers would gain from lower fuel bills as light trucks and large SUVs became more efficient, and from reduced oil consumption. Federal taxpayers would gain from lower fuel costs for the government's vehicle fleet. Commuters and rural drivers who rely on trucks and SUVs would benefit most directly, since those vehicles were the ones exempted from the stricter car standard.

how_it_helps.text: Phases in an average fuel-economy standard for light trucks of 22.5 mpg for model years 2003-2004, 25 mpg for 2005-2006, and 27.5 mpg thereafter, matching the standard long applied to cars.

Extends the legal definition of 'automobile' subject to fuel-economy standards to vehicles up to 10,000 pounds gross vehicle weight starting January 1, 2007, bringing many large SUVs and vans under the rules.
Requires executive agencies to buy new vehicles averaging at least 3 mpg above each vehicle class's fiscal 2001 baseline by September 30, 2003, and 6 mpg above baseline by September 30, 2005.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, especially those selling large volumes of light trucks and SUVs, would bear the cost of redesigning and re-engineering vehicle lines to meet the higher standards. Some of that cost would likely show up in vehicle prices, so buyers of new trucks and large SUVs would pay more upfront in exchange for lower fuel costs over time.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes compliance costs on manufacturers, which would fall partly on buyers of new trucks and large SUVs as higher prices.
The light-truck standard rises to 27.5 mpg only after model year 2006, and trucks built before model year 2003 are exempt, so the near-term savings for buyers are modest.
Extending standards to vehicles up to 10,000 pounds gross vehicle weight could pressure makers and buyers of work trucks and heavy-duty vans used in trades and farming.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — lower fuel costs for owners of trucks and SUVs, the fastest-growing segment of the vehicle market — would likely outweigh higher upfront vehicle prices over the life of the vehicle, and the standards give manufacturers five-plus years of lead time. The main honest cost is that buyers of work-oriented trucks would pay more for vehicles they need for their jobs, and the near-term targets are gradual.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees, each passed it down to a subcommittee, and neither ever advanced it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Olver introduced the Automobile Fuel Economy Act of 2001 on May 10, 2001, with eight original cosponsors from both parties.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Government Reform Committee on the day of introduction.
Within two weeks, both committees referred it to subcommittees — the Subcommittee on Technology and Procurement Policy and the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality.
No further action was taken; the bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers that profit from light trucks and large SUVs, and fuel sellers, were better off because the bill died: the light-truck fuel-economy gap that the bill targeted stayed in place for years afterward.

for.name: Rep. John W. Olver
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to phase in higher fuel-economy standards for light trucks, large SUVs, and the federal fleet.

for.name: 58 House cosponsors (45 Democrats, 12 Republicans, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of raising light-truck fuel-economy standards.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over fuel-economy standards
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never brought it to a markup or vote.

against.name: House Government Reform Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Technology and Procurement Policy; no action followed.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but modest on both sides: 45 of 208 House Democrats and 12 of 223 House Republicans cosponsored, and no chamber-wide vote ever occurred to show where the full parties stood.

industries.industry: Automakers (especially light truck and SUV producers)
industries.note: The bill would have required them to close the fuel-economy gap between trucks and cars, forcing re-engineering of high-margin truck and SUV lines. Their interest in keeping the lower truck standard ran against drivers' interest in cheaper fuel.
More efficient trucks and SUVs mean less gasoline demand per mile driven, cutting into fuel sales. The industry's gain from the bill dying came at the price of drivers' continued fuel costs.
Agencies would have had to buy more efficient vehicles, shifting procurement toward higher-mileage models. Suppliers could still sell to the government but would need to offer more efficient options.
